children: Manish Gangwal of Gulf Oil Lubricants, on why record Q1 FY27 numbers, a rising dividend and an EV stake hike aren't the contradiction they look like

Gulf Oil Lubricants is betting that India's vehicle-ownership curve will decide the next decade. With per-capita car ownership still a fraction of China's or Europe's, Whole Time Director and CFO Manish Gangwal argues the core ICE lubricants business has 15 to 20 years of runway left, even as Gulf Oil simultaneously raises its stake in Tirex, its EV-charging and fluids arm, to 65 per cent. In this interview, Gangwal names the single data point that would force him to rethink that bet, explains why a record Q1 built partly on price hikes doesn't change his volume story, defends a 72 per cent dividend payout alongside an EV pivot, and addresses the governance tension of sitting on both sides of the capital-approval table.

You've publicly argued that India's low per-capita vehicle penetration means the ICE lubricants business will keep growing at the same rate, or faster, for the next decade — even as EVs scale. That's a directional bet with real capital riding on it. What specific data point or EV penetration threshold would tell you that thesis has broken, and that Gulf Oil needs to fundamentally rework its capital allocation rather than treat EV as a side bet?

We believe that while EVs will scale, India's vehicle parc will keep expanding fast enough to offset it at least for the next five to six years. We're at 8-9 cars per 1,000 people versus China's 100-plus and Europe's 300-plus, and we've just crossed the $2,500 per-capita income mark that historically triggers a vehicle-ownership inflection.

The number I'd watch isn't EV market share of new sales, it's total ICE vehicle parc growth turning flat or negative year-on-year, not just decelerating. If new ICE registrations start shrinking in absolute terms rather than just losing share to EVs, that tells me the base is eroding faster than population and income growth can replace it. That's the point we'd shift Tirex and EV fluids to the primary growth engine, and revisit capital allocation between the two businesses. We don’t see that happening in the short term for sure.

Q1 FY27 delivered record volumes, revenue and EBITDA, with lubricant volumes up 14 per cent. But that quarter also saw sharp base oil cost inflation from the Middle East crisis, which you managed through multiple price increases. Realistically, how much of that record performance is genuine volume-led demand versus price increases that customers absorbed only because they had no immediate alternative — and what happens to that growth number the moment the commodity cycle reverses?

Our long-term CAGR has run at roughly 9 per cent for 17 years by growing two-to-three times industry volume growth, so this has been our consistent growth engine over the years, beyond just this quarter. What changed was base oil cost, which forced several price increases to protect per-liter margins. Percentage EBITDA margin looks compressed because revenue jumped on pricing while absolute per-liter margins held up. If crude and base oil normalise, revenue growth moderates back toward the historical 2-3 points above volume growth, and percentage margins should look healthier, since we won't be carrying pass-through cost in the topline. The volume base itself, new accounts we won during the supply disruption should largely stick.

Dividend payout has climbed to 72 per cent even as you continue funding EV charging infrastructure — including raising your Tirex stake to 65 per cent. Is returning that much cash to shareholders now the right call for a company that describes its EV business as the long-term hedge against ICE decline, or does it signal the EV bet still isn't being funded with genuine conviction?

We carry over Rs 1,000 crore of cash on the balance sheet specifically so we can fund inorganic and EV opportunities without touching the payout. Tirex's capacity expansion is being financed off Tirex's own balance sheet, not by diverting lubricant cash flow.

Raising the payout reflects that the core lubricant business is cash-generative and doesn't need all its cash retained. We deliberately avoid cash-burn investment models, and this includes our EV charging business, so it was never going to be capital-hungry the way, say, becoming a charge-point operator would be. If anything, a higher payout alongside a maintained cash buffer signals discipline: we fund EV at the pace the business can absorb, not the pace optics might suggest.

Tirex and EV charging exist as insurance against the lubricants business eventually shrinking. But if EV adoption in India accelerates faster than your own 10-year lubricant-growth thesis assumes, doesn't your hedge's success directly speed up the erosion of the business that still generates almost all your cash — putting you in a race against your own investment?

We believe the lubricant business has at least 15 to 20 years of growth left even after accounting for EVs coming in, because the overall vehicle parc keeps expanding. Besides, charging infrastructure economics work differently; it only becomes meaningful once EV penetration and utilisation are high enough. So, an EV acceleration that hurts lubricants is also the scenario that makes Tirex's addressable market bigger and its unit economics better. It's less a race and more two businesses on the same clock, one winding down as the other scales up.

As both Whole Time Director and CFO, you sit on the board approving capital calls that a CFO would, in a cleaner governance structure, be independently scrutinising rather than co-approving. How do you ensure that decision gets challenged, rather than simply gets signed off by the same person who proposed it?

On something like the Tirex stake increase, it goes through the audit committee and independent directors before it reaches board approval. Before a Board vote, it goes through our Risk Management Committee, which sits independent directors and the MD & CEO alongside me, so the numbers get tested by people who didn't build them. Our Audit Committee reviews the financial and accounting basis separately from the executive team. I'd also say my own mandate has been capital discipline first, that's why we refused the cash burn charging model to begin with.

The Tirex proposal wasn't built on projections alone. By the time the stake increase came to the Board, Tirex had two years of disclosed, growing performance behind it, crossing Rs 100 crore in FY26 revenue. So, the Board was ratifying something with a visible track record and an independent valuation behind it. As the EV book grows, the independent review needs to keep getting stronger, which is a priority at Gulf.

You've set a target of Rs 300-400 crore in EV charging revenue within four to five years, aiming for 10 per cent share of what's projected to become a billion-dollar segment by 2030 — a big leap from a business that only just crossed Rs 100 crore. What's your honest probability that Gulf Oil hits that number given the scale of EV-native and auto-OEM competition already chasing the same charging infrastructure market, and what's the more likely outcome if it doesn't?

We view the Rs 300–400 crore target as a calculated growth ambition. Based on the scale we have already achieved and the investments underway, we believe there is a high probability of achieving it over the next four to five years.

Tirex has already crossed Rs 100 crore in revenue, giving us a meaningful base from which to scale. We have established capabilities in high-power DC charging, strong OEM and fleet relationships, and are investing in additional manufacturing capacity and product breadth. These are tangible advantages as India moves from early EV adoption towards much larger commercial and fleet electrification.

We are also realistic about competition. We do not need to win the entire charging market; our objective is to build a profitable, defensible position in the segments where our technology, reliability, localisation and relationships give us an advantage. The Rs 300–400 crore opportunity represents roughly 3–4x our current revenue over four to five years, which we believe is a disciplined growth trajectory in a market that is expected to expand significantly.

There are always uncertainties and the possibility of the market developing at a slower pace than anticipated. We have always factored such scenarios and are clear that our capital allocation will remain disciplined. We will continue to prioritise returns over chasing headline revenue, calibrate capacity and investment accordingly, while continuing to build our EV value chain across Tirex, Electrifee and Indra.
Savi Khanna
BW Reporters Assistant Editor, BW Businessworld
